questions.stem: Lithium reacts gently with water, sodium reacts vigorously, and potassium reacts so vigorously it catches fire. If rubidium (below potassium in Group 1) were added to water, what would you predict?

options.text: It would react less vigorously than potassium because heavier elements are less reactive
It would not react at all because it is too heavy
It would react even more vigorously than potassium, possibly exploding
It would react at the same rate as potassium

questions.explanation: Reactivity increases down Group 1 because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost. Rubidium's outer electron is in a higher energy level with more shielding than potassium's, so it would react even more vigorously with water — likely causing an explosion.

questions.stem: A student cuts a piece of sodium and notices the shiny surface quickly turns dull. What is happening and what does this tell us about storing alkali metals?

options.text: The sodium is melting; it should be stored in a freezer
The sodium is reacting with oxygen in the air to form an oxide layer; it should be stored under oil
The sodium is dissolving in moisture; it should be stored in water
The sodium is changing colour naturally; no special storage is needed

questions.explanation: Freshly cut sodium is shiny but rapidly reacts with oxygen and moisture in the air, forming a dull oxide layer. Alkali metals are so reactive that they must be stored under oil to prevent contact with air and water. Storing in water would cause a dangerous reaction.

questions.stem: Sodium reacts with water to produce sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas. If you tested the resulting solution with universal indicator, what colour would you expect?

options.text: Red, because the solution is acidic
Green, because the solution is neutral
Purple/blue, because the solution is alkaline
Orange, because the solution is weakly acidic

questions.explanation: Sodium reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide (NaOH), which is a strong alkali. This is why Group 1 elements are called the 'alkali metals' — they produce alkaline solutions when they react with water. Universal indicator turns purple/blue in alkaline solutions (pH > 7).

questions.stem: Compared to iron, sodium has a much lower melting point and density. A student concludes that all metals must have low melting points and densities. Why is this conclusion incorrect?

options.text: Sodium is not actually a metal
Alkali metals are atypical metals with lower melting points and densities than most metals due to weaker metallic bonding
Iron is not actually a metal
All metals have the same melting points and densities

questions.explanation: Alkali metals are atypical compared to most metals. They have lower melting points, lower densities (lithium, sodium, and potassium float on water), and are soft enough to cut with a knife. This is because they have weaker metallic bonding with only one outer electron contributing to the 'sea of delocalised electrons', unlike transition metals which have much stronger metallic bonds.

questions.stem: When lithium burns in air, it produces a white solid. A student dissolves this solid in water and tests the pH. The pH is 13. What is the white solid, and what compound forms in solution?

options.text: Lithium chloride; lithium chloride solution
Lithium oxide; lithium hydroxide solution
Lithium carbonate; carbonic acid solution
Lithium sulfate; sulfuric acid solution

questions.explanation: When lithium burns in air, it reacts with oxygen to form lithium oxide (Li₂O). When lithium oxide dissolves in water, it forms lithium hydroxide (LiOH), a strong alkali with a high pH of 13. The equation is: Li₂O + H₂O → 2LiOH.
